qs.q: A toxicology consult team evaluates a drug with a very low therapeutic index (TI). Which clinical characteristic is most definitive of this category?
o: One hundred percent oral bioavailability regardless of metabolism
A narrow margin between efficacy and toxicity requiring monitoring
A wide margin of safety between lethal and effective doses
Complete elimination exclusively via non-renal metabolic pathways
qs.e: A low therapeutic index means there is a narrow margin between the effective dose and the toxic or lethal dose, necessitating regular therapeutic drug monitoring. High therapeutic index drugs possess wide safety margins.
qs.s: Master Pharmacokinetics, Dynamics & Antimicrobial Drugs: MCQs

qs.q: What physiological characteristic of lithium contributes significantly to its narrow therapeutic index and toxicity risk?
o: It is completely cleared within two hours
It undergoes rapid hepatic phase I oxidation
It is reabsorbed extensively by the renal tubules
It binds extensively to plasma albumin proteins
qs.e: Lithium is excreted by the kidney, but 85% of it is reabsorbed, making salt intake, hydration status, and drug interactions critical factors in toxicity. It does not primarily bind extensively to albumin.

o: Margin of safety for the drug
qs.e: TI = TD50/ED50 or LD50/ED50. A higher TI indicates a wider margin between therapeutic and toxic doses, meaning greater safety.

qs.q: A drug has an ED50 of 10mg and a TD50 of 100mg. What is its therapeutic index?
qs.e: Therapeutic Index = TD50/ED50 = 100/10 = 10. A higher therapeutic index indicates a wider margin of safety between therapeutic and toxic doses.

qs.q: Which drug has the narrowest therapeutic index requiring routine TDM? ---
qs.e: Digoxin has a very narrow therapeutic window, so routine therapeutic drug monitoring is required.

qs.q: : The LD50 of a new compound is determined to be 200 mg/kg, while its ED50 is 20 mg/kg. What is the Therapeutic Index (TI) of this drug?
qs.e: The Therapeutic Index is calculated as LD50/ED50. In this case: 200/20 = 10. A TI of 10 indicates the drug has a reasonable margin of safety, as the lethal dose is 10 times higher than the effective dose. Drugs with higher TI values are generally considered safer.

ai.subject: Pharmacology
ai.summary: The therapeutic index (TI) quantifies how close a drug's effective dose is to its toxic dose, guiding safe prescribing and monitoring. A narrow TI demands careful dose titration and often blood‑level checks.

sections.p: TI is the ratio of a drug’s toxic dose (TD50) to its effective dose (ED50). A high TI means a wide safety margin; a low TI signals a narrow margin requiring vigilance.
b: TI = TD50 / ED50
Narrow TI drugs need therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)

sections.p: Clinical severity is staged by symptom intensity and laboratory levels relative to therapeutic range.
b: Mild: symptoms absent, levels within target
Moderate: early toxicity signs, levels slightly above target
Severe: overt toxicity, organ dysfunction

sections.p: Factors that shrink the TI or raise drug levels.
b: Renal impairment (e.g., digoxin, lithium)
Electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia ↑ digoxin toxicity)
Drug interactions (e.g., NSAIDs ↓ lithium clearance)
Age, pregnancy, malnutrition

sections.p: Symptoms reflect the organ systems most vulnerable to the drug’s excess.
b: Cardiac: arrhythmias (digoxin)
Neurologic: tremor, confusion, seizures (lithium)
GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea

sections.p: Targeted tests confirm drug levels and assess organ impact.

t.b: Is the level within the therapeutic window? High level indicates toxicity; low level suggests under‑dosing.
Is clearance reduced? Impaired kidneys raise levels of renally cleared narrow‑TI drugs.
Are electrolytes abnormal? Low K+ potentiates digoxin toxicity.
Are there arrhythmias or characteristic changes? Confirms cardiac toxicity.

b: Severe arrhythmia or heart block
Seizures or coma
Renal failure worsening drug accumulation

sections.p: Stop or adjust the offending drug, treat toxicity, and monitor.
b: Discontinue or halve dose; consider alternative class with wider TI
Use specific antidotes when available (e.g., digoxin‑specific Fab fragments)
Supportive care: IV fluids, electrolyte correction, seizure control
Re‑measure drug level after intervention

sections.p: Regular monitoring and patient education keep levels in range.
b: Schedule routine TDM for narrow‑TI drugs
Educate on signs of toxicity and importance of adherence
Adjust dose when renal function or electrolytes change
Therapeutic window – clinical range of safe concentrations, not a ratio
Dose‑response curve – shows effect magnitude, not safety margin
Single trough level may be normal while peak level is toxic
Laboratory interference (e.g., hemolysis) can falsely lower measured lithium

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid decline in renal function with narrow‑TI drug on board

faq.q: Why do some drugs have a narrow therapeutic index?
faq.a: Their mechanism affects vital systems at doses close to therapeutic levels, so a small increase causes toxicity.

faq.q: Is therapeutic drug monitoring required for all drugs?
faq.a: Only for drugs with a narrow TI, unpredictable pharmacokinetics, or high toxicity risk.

faq.q: Can I rely on symptoms alone to detect toxicity?
faq.a: No; early toxicity may be asymptomatic, so blood levels and labs are essential.
